properties.title: AIO Fact Check
properties.content: Question: can celiac disease cause thyroid problems Answer: Yes, celiac disease can increase the risk of developing thyroid problems, particularly autoimmune thyroid diseases like Hashimoto's thyroiditis and Graves' disease. Both celiac disease and these thyroid conditions are autoimmune disorders, meaning the body's immune system mistakenly attacks its own tissues. Here's why:: - Shared Genetic Predisposition: Both celiac disease and autoimmune thyroid diseases share some of the same genetic risk factors, making individuals with celiac disease more susceptible to developing thyroid problems. - Autoimmune Nature: Celiac disease, Hashimoto's, and Graves' disease are all autoimmune disorders. This means that the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own tissues. In celiac disease, the small intestine is targeted, while in thyroid diseases, the thyroid gland is affected. - Increased Risk: Studies have shown that people with celiac disease have a higher chance of developing autoimmune thyroid disease compared to the general population, according to the Kaplan Center for Integrative Medicine. - Possible Gut-Thyroid Axis: There's emerging research suggesting a possible link between the gut and the thyroid gland, known as the gut-thyroid axis. Chronic inflammation in the gut, as seen in celiac disease, may contribute to the development or progression of thyroid autoimmunity. - Molecular Mimicry: In some cases, the immune system may mistakenly attack the thyroid gland because it perceives similarities between gluten (a protein in wheat, barley, and rye) and thyroid tissue. This phenomenon is called molecular mimicry. - Vitamin D Deficiency: Celiac disease can lead to vitamin D deficiency due to impaired absorption. Vitamin D plays a role in immune function, and deficiency is also linked to autoimmune thyroid diseases. Important points to remember:: - Not all individuals with celiac disease will develop thyroid problems. - Testing for thyroid disorders should be considered in individuals with celiac disease, says the Kaplan Center for Integrative Medicine. - If you have celiac disease and experience symptoms of hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism, it's crucial to consult with your doctor . - Managing celiac disease with a strict gluten-free diet is essential, even if you don't have diagnosed thyroid problems, as it can help reduce overall inflammation and potentially improve thyroid health, according to Amy Myers MD.

Question: can celiac disease cause thyroid problems

Answer: Yes, celiac disease can increase the risk of developing thyroid problems, particularly autoimmune thyroid diseases like Hashimoto's thyroiditis and Graves' disease. Both celiac disease and these thyroid conditions are autoimmune disorders, meaning the body's immune system mistakenly attacks its own tissues.
Here's why::
- Shared Genetic Predisposition: Both celiac disease and autoimmune thyroid diseases share some of the same genetic risk factors, making individuals with celiac disease more susceptible to developing thyroid problems.
- Autoimmune Nature: Celiac disease, Hashimoto's, and Graves' disease are all autoimmune disorders. This means that the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own tissues. In celiac disease, the small intestine is targeted, while in thyroid diseases, the thyroid gland is affected.
- Increased Risk: Studies have shown that people with celiac disease have a higher chance of developing autoimmune thyroid disease compared to the general population, according to the Kaplan Center for Integrative Medicine.
- Possible Gut-Thyroid Axis: There's emerging research suggesting a possible link between the gut and the thyroid gland, known as the gut-thyroid axis. Chronic inflammation in the gut, as seen in celiac disease, may contribute to the development or progression of thyroid autoimmunity.
- Molecular Mimicry: In some cases, the immune system may mistakenly attack the thyroid gland because it perceives similarities between gluten (a protein in wheat, barley, and rye) and thyroid tissue. This phenomenon is called molecular mimicry.
- Vitamin D Deficiency: Celiac disease can lead to vitamin D deficiency due to impaired absorption. Vitamin D plays a role in immune function, and deficiency is also linked to autoimmune thyroid diseases.
Important points to remember::
- Not all individuals with celiac disease will develop thyroid problems.
- Testing for thyroid disorders should be considered in individuals with celiac disease, says the Kaplan Center for Integrative Medicine.
- If you have celiac disease and experience symptoms of hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism, it's crucial to consult with your doctor .
- Managing celiac disease with a strict gluten-free diet is essential, even if you don't have diagnosed thyroid problems, as it can help reduce overall inflammation and potentially improve thyroid health, according to Amy Myers MD.
